prompt: A gate breaks the build on every finding, including advisories with no fixed version. Why does that end up less safe than a gate that warns on those?

choices.text: Breaking builds slows the pipeline down
choices.why: A broken build is not slower; the damage is to what people learn from it.

choices.text: Red stops meaning anything, and one line switches it off
choices.why: Right. allow_failure, continue-on-error or a commented stage, and the true finding then reaches nobody.

choices.text: Scanners report fewer findings when they break the build
choices.why: The scanner reports the same findings whatever the pipeline does with them.

choices.text: Advisories without a fix are false positives
choices.why: They are real; the point is that nobody can act on them by changing a pin.

prompt: Match each line to where it turns a gate into a decoration.

pairs.right: the end of a command in a shell stage

right_distractors: the exceptions file of the composition gate

prompt: Which findings break the build whether or not the rule "only what the person who broke it can fix, now" would say so?

choices.text: A secret in a pushed commit
choices.why: Right. Its owner can always act, by revoking it, and every minute costs.

choices.text: A check that did not run to the end
choices.why: Right. Silence is not a pass; this is failing closed.

choices.text: An advisory rated critical with no fixed version
choices.why: Severity does not create a fix. It warns, and somebody owns it.

choices.text: A finding in code older than a year
choices.why: Old code is the case baselines exist for; age alone breaks nothing.

prompt: Which exit status does a stage return, in the lesson's pipeline, to pass with a warning?
Why is a warning 3 and not 2?

choices.text: 2 is reserved by POSIX for warnings from the shell
choices.why: No such reservation exists; the shell said 127 for a missing command.

choices.text: Python exits 2 on a bad option
choices.why: Right: a typo in a flag would then pass as a warning. A crash has to land on a status the pipeline treats as a break.

choices.text: ZAP exits 3 for warnings, and the pipeline copies it
choices.why: ZAP exits 2 for warnings; dast.sh translates it to 3.

choices.text: Bash cannot read statuses below 3 inside a while loop
choices.why: The loop reads any status; the choice is about what failures produce.

prompt: ZAP's baseline scan exits 3 when the scan itself could not finish. What does the lesson's `ci/dast.sh` turn that into?

choices.text: 3, a warning, because the number is the same
choices.why: The case sends only ZAP's 2 to 3; any other status goes to 1.

choices.text: 0, since a scan that did not finish found nothing
choices.why: Finding nothing because nothing ran is the pass this lesson refuses.

choices.text: 1, a break
choices.why: Right. Everything but 0 and 2 goes to 1: the stage fails closed.

choices.text: It retries the scan once before deciding
choices.why: Nothing in the script retries; it maps the status and exits.

prompt: Lesson 4's scan told ZAP to exit 0 on warnings with a one-letter flag, which this lesson removes. The flag is ___
Why does `ci/sca.sh` write pip-audit's report to a file made by `mktemp` instead of `audit.json` in the project?

choices.text: pip-audit refuses to write inside a git repository
choices.why: It wrote audit.json into the project without complaint in the first version.

choices.text: So no earlier run's report ever stands in for one that was not written
choices.why: Right. On the laptop, a failed run passed on yesterday's report.

choices.text: Temporary files are faster to read
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The CI clone is read-only
choices.why: The CI's clone is writable; the defect showed on the laptop.

prompt: Somebody adds the line `PYSEC-2026-1475 2026-11-20` to `ci/exceptions.txt`, with no reason after the date. What happens on the next run?

choices.text: The exception holds, since the date is in the future
choices.why: The line never becomes an exception: it does not unpack into three fields.

choices.text: The gate skips the line as a comment
choices.why: Only lines starting with # are comments.

choices.text: The gate warns that a reason is missing and passes
choices.why: There is no such warning in the code; it raises.

choices.text: Python raises; the gate exits 1 and breaks
choices.why: Right. An exception nobody explained is refused, and nothing was written to refuse it.

prompt: With `werkzeug==3.0.1` pinned beside `flask==3.1.3`, the composition stage exited 1. Why?

choices.text: werkzeug 3.0.1 has advisories with fixed versions
choices.why: It does, but pip-audit never got that far: it could not install the set.

choices.text: The two pins conflict, so no report was written
choices.why: Right. A file nobody can install is not a file without advisories.

choices.text: The gate breaks on any downgrade
choices.why: The gate reads advisories; it knows nothing of versions going down.

choices.text: The tests failed first and stopped the run
choices.why: This was ci/sca.sh run on its own, and the error is pip's resolver.

prompt: Why does `judge()` take `today` as a parameter rather than reading the clock?

choices.text: To fix the day in the tests
choices.why: Right. The tests use 14 October, check both sides of a date and pass on any day.

choices.text: Because the CI server has no clock
choices.why: It has one; the shell scripts print timings from it.

choices.text: So exceptions are judged in UTC
choices.why: The parameter is a date, and the program passes the local one.

choices.text: pip-audit puts the date in its report
choices.why: The report carries no date; the gate supplies it.

prompt: On the branch that moved Jinja2 back to 3.1.4, how many distinct advisories did the gate list as BREAKS?
An advisory with a fixed version is published against pytest, which only the tests use. What does the gate do, and is it right by the lesson's rule?

choices.text: It warns, because development dependencies never ship
choices.why: The gate reads both files the same way, and pytest runs in the pipeline with its credentials.

choices.text: It passes, because pip-audit reads requirements.txt alone
choices.why: sca.sh passes both files to pip-audit.

choices.text: It breaks: one pin, movable now by whoever pushed
choices.why: Right. Fixable now by the person who pushed, whatever the dependency is for.

choices.text: It breaks, but the rule says it should warn
choices.why: The rule asks whether the pusher can fix it now; here they can.

prompt: The ecdsa branch passed with a warning. What made the advisory not apply to the planned use, according to its own text?

choices.text: The advisory concerns the P-384 curve, and the service uses P-256
choices.why: It names P-256 itself.

choices.text: A fix is due in the next release
choices.why: The project says there is no planned fix.

choices.text: Verification is unaffected, and the service only verifies
choices.why: Right. Without a private key to sign with, there is nothing for the timing leak to reveal.

choices.text: Timing attacks need physical access to the server
choices.why: The advisory says nothing of the kind; the reading turns on signing versus verifying.

prompt: Put the life of an exception in order.
items: a line with the advisory, a date and a reason is committed
the advisory passes, logged as excepted
in its last week, the gate warns
the day after the date, the finding breaks the build again
a new commit with a new date and reason renews it

prompt: The exception lines name advisories, not the package. What follows when a fourth advisory is published against Jinja2 3.1.4?

choices.text: It is covered, since the package is excepted
choices.why: Nothing excepts a package; each line is one advisory id.

choices.text: It warns until somebody adds a line
choices.why: It has a fixed version or not; with one, it breaks.

choices.text: The gate refuses the whole exceptions file
choices.why: The other lines still hold; only the new advisory is unexcepted.

choices.text: It breaks, if it has a fix
choices.why: Right. A decision about three advisories says nothing about a fourth.

prompt: Match each case to its verdict and reason.

pairs.right: break: its owner can revoke it at once
warn: kept visible, scoped out when it becomes noise

pairs.left: B108 in a function nothing calls
pairs.right: break: fixable now, and unreachability is not checked

pairs.left: an advisory with no fixed version
pairs.right: warn: somebody owns it and reads it

right_distractors: pass: it is in last year's baseline

prompt: Rule 10031 is a proven false positive on `/search`. Why not set it to IGNORE in `ci/zap-rules.conf`?

choices.text: IGNORE silences the rule on every page, the next one included
choices.why: Right. OUTOFSCOPE for /search is the precise tool when the warning becomes noise.

choices.text: ZAP refuses IGNORE for passive rules
choices.why: IGNORE is one of the levels the configuration accepts.

choices.text: IGNORE would make the nightly run fail
choices.why: It drops the rule; the run would pass with no warning.

choices.text: The rule might stop being a false positive tomorrow on /search
choices.why: The response proves it false there; the risk is the other pages.

prompt: After the webhook branch was deleted from the CI server, where was the pushed secret still to be found?

choices.text: Nowhere: deleting the branch on the server removed its commits with it
choices.why: Deleting a branch removes a name; the commit stays until Git collects it, and the run's clone keeps a copy.

choices.text: Only in the developer's laptop
choices.why: The server and the run's clone hold it too.

choices.text: In the server's objects until collected, and in the run's clone
choices.why: Right. Which is why the response starts with revoking it.

choices.text: In the image the build stage pushed
choices.why: The run stopped at the first stage; no image was built.

prompt: What does an exception line carry that a line in a baseline does not?

choices.text: The rule that found it
choices.why: A baseline records the finding, rule included.

choices.text: A date, a reason and, through its commit, an owner
choices.why: Right. A baseline has no day on which the decision is looked at again.

choices.text: The file and line of the finding
choices.why: Baselines carry those; they are how a finding is matched.

choices.text: A severity score
choices.why: Neither carries one in this lesson.

prompt: The owner of an exception is not a field of the file. The Git command that names the commit behind each of its lines is git ___
A team adds Semgrep to a five-year-old service, and the first run reports 300 findings. Which first move follows the lesson?

choices.text: Break the build on all 300 until they are fixed
choices.why: Nobody pushing on Tuesday wrote them; the gate is switched off by Thursday.

choices.text: Warn on all 300 and break on nothing
choices.why: The next real finding is lost among three hundred old ones.

choices.text: Write one exception per finding, each with a date
choices.why: Three hundred dated decisions is a baseline with extra paperwork, and they all expire together.

choices.text: Baseline today, break on new ones, and own the old
choices.why: Right. New findings follow the rule, and the old ones are debt with an owner and a budget.
